stops.title: 1. The Old Port — La Rochelle's gateway
stops.credit: Wikimedia Commons — CC licence shown on the file page
stops.text: Begin at the entrance to the Vieux-Port, where three medieval towers once controlled access to La Rochelle: the Tour de la Chaîne on the south side, the Tour Saint-Nicolas opposite it, and the Tour de la Lanterne farther west. The harbour is the key to understanding the city. La Rochelle grew as a maritime trading town from the medieval period, and its position on the Atlantic made it prosperous, strategically important and repeatedly contested. The two great towers at the entrance are unusually well preserved because, after the city's defeat in the Great Siege of 1627–1628, the royal government demolished much of the landward fortifications but spared the seafront towers. Look across the water and imagine the heavy chain that was once stretched between the Chain Tower and Saint-Nicolas Tower at night to close the harbour. This is also a good place simply to appreciate the scale of the old harbour and the way the modern town still wraps around its medieval core.
stops.tip: Flat. Exterior viewing only; entering the towers involves stairs and is optional.

stops.title: 2. Tour de la Chaîne and Cours des Dames
stops.text: The Tour de la Chaîne dates from the late fourteenth century and was one half of the mechanism that closed the harbour. The chain itself was attached here and stretched to the much larger Tour Saint-Nicolas. The tower later had other uses, including as a powder store. Today it forms one of the most recognisable silhouettes of La Rochelle. Walk a little along the Cours des Dames and look back toward the tower: you can see how the medieval defensive structure now sits comfortably among cafés, restaurants and the everyday life of the port. The contrast is part of La Rochelle's appeal — this is not a museum city frozen in the past.
stops.tip: Flat, with good places to pause.

stops.title: 3. Tour de la Lanterne — the lighthouse and prison
stops.credit: Wikimedia Commons — CC licence shown on the file page
stops.text: The Tour de la Lanterne is the oldest surviving lighthouse tower on the Atlantic coast of France. The present tower was built in the fifteenth century, replacing an earlier structure. Its name comes from the lantern once lit at the top to guide ships. But the tower also became a prison, and its walls preserve graffiti and inscriptions made by prisoners, particularly in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. For our walking tour, the important thing is the exterior: the tower marks the western edge of the historic harbour and the beginning of the old seaward defences. If you decide to go inside, treat it as an optional extra rather than part of the timed walk because the tower involves substantial stair climbing.
stops.tip: Flat outside. Interior is an optional stair-heavy detour.

stops.title: 4. Grosse Horloge — from city gate to town clock
stops.credit: Jean-Christophe BENOIST / Wikimedia Commons — CC BY 3.0
stops.text: Now pass beneath the Grosse Horloge, one of La Rochelle's defining landmarks. It began as a fortified gateway in the medieval wall separating the town from the port. Originally there were separate openings for carts and pedestrians. In the fifteenth century a clock and bell were added. Later, as traffic increased, the openings were combined, and in the eighteenth century the upper part was rebuilt in the elegant form you see today. Notice the change in character as you pass through: on one side is the waterfront and on the other the dense historic town. The gateway is therefore more than a pretty monument — it is a surviving physical boundary between two parts of medieval La Rochelle.
stops.tip: Flat and pedestrian-friendly. Pause on either side rather than under the arch if busy.

stops.title: 5. The arcaded streets — practical elegance
stops.credit: Guilhem Vellut / Wikimedia Commons — CC licence shown on the file page
stops.text: As you walk through the centre, look down the streets rather than only at individual monuments. La Rochelle is famous for its arcades — covered passages created beneath houses along important commercial streets. They protected pedestrians and shopkeepers from Atlantic rain and summer sun, while also providing valuable sheltered space for commerce. The town's prosperity is visible in the mixture of buildings: medieval timber-framed houses survive beside grander seventeenth- and eighteenth-century stone townhouses. This is one of the pleasures of La Rochelle: the historic character is spread through ordinary streets rather than concentrated in a single monument.
stops.tip: Very flat. Take your time and look into side streets.

stops.title: 6. Hôtel de Ville — power, independence and the Great Siege
stops.credit: Wikimedia Commons — CC licence shown on the file page
stops.text: La Rochelle's Hôtel de Ville has an extraordinary claim: the city has had a town hall here since 1298, making it the oldest French town hall still in use. The building you see was largely rebuilt around 1490 in a deliberately fortified style, with crenellations, machicolations and a corner tower. That appearance tells us something about the political confidence of medieval La Rochelle. The city enjoyed unusual municipal independence and became a major Protestant stronghold during the Reformation. The most dramatic chapter came in 1627–1628, when royal forces under Cardinal Richelieu besieged the Protestant city. The mayor Jean Guiton became a symbol of resistance. Look for his statue in the square. The building was badly damaged by fire in 2013 and reopened after major restoration in 2019.
stops.tip: Flat. The square is a good rest point.

stops.title: 7. Renaissance La Rochelle — merchants, money and the Atlantic
stops.credit: Guilhem Vellut / Wikimedia Commons — CC licence shown on the file page
stops.text: This part of the old town is where La Rochelle's commercial success becomes architectural. Wealthy merchants and shipowners built substantial houses, often with elaborate façades, courtyards and carved details. The city's Atlantic connections brought goods, people and ideas from far beyond the immediate region. That prosperity also had a darker side. La Rochelle was involved in Atlantic colonial trade, including the slave trade, and several merchant families accumulated wealth through it. The city's museums and heritage interpretation do not hide that history. When looking at the grand houses, it is worth remembering that impressive architecture can record both commercial achievement and uncomfortable sources of wealth.
stops.tip: Flat. This is an optional shorter stop if time is running short.

stops.title: 8. Saint-Louis Cathedral and Protestant La Rochelle
stops.credit: Wikimedia Commons — CC licence shown on the file page
stops.text: Saint-Louis Cathedral is a useful reminder that La Rochelle's religious history was anything but simple. During the Reformation the city became a major centre of French Protestantism. After the Great Siege and the defeat of the Huguenot city, Catholic institutions were restored and the religious landscape changed dramatically. The present cathedral occupies a site associated with that transition. Inside, if open, look up at the nineteenth-century dome paintings associated with William Bouguereau. Even if you remain outside, the building helps explain why the story of La Rochelle is not just one of ships and merchants but also of religious conflict, royal power and changing French identity.
stops.tip: Flat. Interior visit optional and subject to opening hours.

stops.title: 9. Central Market — La Rochelle alive today
stops.credit: Patrick Despoix / Wikimedia Commons — CC BY-SA 3.0
stops.text: The Marché Central is a change of pace: instead of looking at a monument, listen to the city. The present market hall dates from 1834 and is still a working food market. Its architecture — large glazed areas, zinc roofing and a small clock tower — is deliberately practical rather than monumental. On market mornings the surrounding streets fill with stalls as well. For visitors, this is a chance to see La Rochelle functioning as a living town rather than as a heritage display. If your cruise stop falls on a market morning, allow extra time here: browsing is part of the experience.
stops.tip: Completely flat. Market activity may make the area crowded.

stops.title: 10. Back through the old town — the final view
stops.credit: Wikimedia Commons — CC licence shown on the file page
stops.text: On the return through the old town, notice how little you have needed to climb. That is one of the pleasures of La Rochelle: the historic centre is compact and predominantly level. Look for the combination of timber framing, pale local stone, shutters, arcades and narrow streets. These details are the connective tissue between the major monuments you have visited. As you return toward the harbour, the Grosse Horloge provides a useful visual anchor. From here you can choose either to return directly to the port or repeat part of the waterfront at your own pace.
stops.tip: Flat. This is the flexible finish: return to the ship or explore a little longer.
